\section[fortitūdō, fortitūdinis]{fortitūdō, fortitūdinis — courage, bravery}

\label{lesson:LA-C509-fortitudo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for vigorous, then the Latin for diligent.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fortitūdō, fortitūdinis}
\textbf{fortitūdō, fortitūdinis} — \textquotedblleft{}courage, bravery\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mīlitēs magnā fortitūdine pugnant.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The soldiers fight with great courage.}
\end{quote}

Feminine, third declension, from \emph{fortis}. One of the four great virtues of ancient ethics. English \emph{fortitude}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{fortitūdō} is built on \emph{fortis} \textquotedblleft{}strong, brave\textquotedblright{} with \emph{-tūdō} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB). English \emph{fortitude} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{fortitūdō, fortitūdinis}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{fortitūdō, fortitūdinis}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{fortitūdō, fortitūdinis}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for vigorous, then the Latin for diligent, then say \emph{fortitūdō, fortitūdinis} again
\end{itemize}

\section[audācia, audāciae]{audācia, audāciae — boldness, daring}

\label{lesson:LA-C509-audacia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for diligent, then the Latin for courage.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: audācia, audāciae}
\textbf{audācia, audāciae} — \textquotedblleft{}boldness, daring\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Audācia nautae omnēs servat.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The sailor's daring saves everyone.}
\end{quote}

Feminine, first declension, from \emph{audāx}. Often in a bad sense: recklessness, impudence. English \emph{audacity}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{audācia} is built on \emph{audāx} \textquotedblleft{}bold\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{audeō} \textquotedblleft{}to dare\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB). English \emph{audacity} comes from the same adjective.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[temerārius, temerāria, temerārium]{temerārius, temerāria, temerārium — rash, reckless}

\label{lesson:LA-C509-temerarius}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for courage, then the Latin for boldness.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: temerārius, temerāria, temerārium}
\textbf{temerārius, temerāria, temerārium} — \textquotedblleft{}rash, reckless\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Iuvenis temerārius in flūmen altum salit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The rash young man jumps into the deep river.}
\end{quote}

From the adverb \emph{temere} — blindly, by chance. English \emph{temerity} comes from the related \emph{temeritās}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{temerārius} is built on the adverb \emph{temere} \textquotedblleft{}blindly, by chance\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB). English \emph{temerity} comes from the related \emph{temeritās}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[cōnstāns, cōnstantis]{cōnstāns, cōnstantis — steadfast, consistent}

\label{lesson:LA-C509-constans}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for boldness, then the Latin for rash.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: cōnstāns, cōnstantis}
\textbf{cōnstāns, cōnstantis} — \textquotedblleft{}steadfast, consistent\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Amīcus cōnstāns in perīculīs nōn fugit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{A steadfast friend does not run away in danger.}
\end{quote}

One ending. The present participle of \emph{cōnstō} — to stand firm. English \emph{constant}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{cōnstāns} is the present participle of \emph{cōnstō} \textquotedblleft{}to stand firm\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{con-} and \emph{stō} \textquotedblleft{}to stand\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB). English \emph{constant} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[prūdentia, prūdentiae]{prūdentia, prūdentiae — good sense, prudence}

\label{lesson:LA-C509-prudentia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for rash, then the Latin for steadfast.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: prūdentia, prūdentiae}
\textbf{prūdentia, prūdentiae} — \textquotedblleft{}good sense, prudence\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Prūdentiā patris familia servātur.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The family is saved by the father's good sense.}
\end{quote}

Feminine, first declension, from \emph{prūdēns}, a short form of \emph{prōvidēns} — foreseeing. English \emph{prudence}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{prūdentia} is built on \emph{prūdēns} \textquotedblleft{}wise\textquotedblright{}, a shortened \emph{prōvidēns} \textquotedblleft{}foreseeing\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB links it with \emph{prōvidentia}). English \emph{prudence} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
